html:
The Indian Forest Act of 1878 was a colonial law that gave the British government control over India's forests and fenced off huge areas from the people who had lived from them.

The railways needed timber for sleepers, and the state wanted to manage forests for revenue. A forest department was set up in 1864 under the German forester Dietrich Brandis, and a first act passed in 1865. The 1878 act went much further:

  • It divided forests into reserved, protected and village forests.
  • In reserved forests, old customary rights to graze, gather and cut became privileges the state could grant or refuse.
  • It restricted shifting cultivation, hunting and the collection of forest produce.

The people hit hardest were forest dwelling tribes, the Adivasi, along with herders and villagers. Many rose up in forest rebellions in the decades after. A new act in 1927 kept the same approach, and independent India inherited it.

The long fight over forests resurfaced in the Chipko movement of the 1970s and led to the Forest Rights Act of 2006, which restored some rights to forest communities.
sum: The Indian Forest Act of 1878 was a colonial law that gave the British government control over India's forests and fenced off huge areas from the people who had lived from them.
